2026, arXiv preprint arXiv:2605.12729v2 [cs.NI], version of 15 June 2026 (p. 1, margin stamp). A survey-style journal manuscript not yet published in a peer-reviewed venue at extraction time; the search window itself runs to May 2026 (SS I.C, p. 4).

LLMs are increasingly used across NetOps and AIOps for incident investigation, root-cause analysis, configuration synthesis and limited self-healing, turning fragmented operational work into a single loop that reads, reasons and acts near live control surfaces (Abstract and SS I, pp. 1-2). This shift collides with growing operational burden (breadth of tool surface, velocity of change, volume of interruption) in SRE organisations that aim to minimise detection and recovery times (SS I, p. 2), yet the field lacks shared terms for autonomy, a stable set of evaluation tasks, and a threat model matching real operational tool surfaces (SS I, p. 2). The survey's core question is how to design, evaluate and govern NetOps/AIOps agents so as to maintain or maximise reliability and security while reducing operational burden, improving outcomes such as diagnostic and mitigation times under explicit safety constraints (SS I.A(d), p. 3). Its central thesis: operational reliability comes not chiefly from the model but from the machinery around it - typed tool interfaces, provenance-aware retrieval, budgets, least privilege, and verification gates at the write boundary (Abstract, p. 1).

Not a new system but a contract-centred taxonomy that treats agentic NetOps/AIOps as constrained operational control (SS I.D, p. 6; Table I, p. 7). Autonomy is modelled as a ladder of four rungs - read-only copilot, tool-grounded analyst, write-limited planner-executor, and closed-loop self-healing controller (Fig. 5, p. 17) - each written as an operational assurance contract C_k = (T_k, R_k, G_k, U_k, B_k) over permitted tools, required evidence, non-bypassable gates, rollout/rollback/audit protocol, and budgets (SS IV.A, Eq. 12, pp. 16-17; Table III, p. 18). Supporting primitives include typed evidence traces E as first-class, scoreable outputs (Eq. 3, pp. 3-4; Eq. 14, p. 17), explicit budgets and stop rules (SS III.A, Eqs. 8-10, pp. 13-14), a non-bypassable 'verification wall' between proposal and execution (SS III.C, Eq. 11, p. 15), a gated planner-executor loop (Algorithm 1, p. 16), and a reviewable human-approval bundle of diff, preconditions, checks, canary plan, rollback triggers and evidence pointers (Eq. 19 and Fig. 6, p. 19). The copilot rung - the thesis-relevant role - is defined as read-only evidence compression and navigation whose success criteria are faster evidence location and fewer missed signals, with bounded tool calls (Pattern A, SS IV.F, p. 20; Table III, p. 18).

Secondary study: a structured review protocol with explicit, reproducible scope (SS I.C, pp. 4-5). Searches covered ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, USENIX proceedings, arXiv, Google Scholar, IETF documents, NIST material and selected standards/project pages, mainly for January 2020 - May 2026, with earlier foundational work retained (p. 4). Queries were organised into six strands (NetOps; AIOps/SRE; LLM-agent; evaluation; safety/security; standards/practice) and screened in two stages (title/abstract/venue/keywords, then full text against the survey question) using explicit inclusion and exclusion conditions, deduplication, and preference for peer-reviewed over preprint versions (pp. 4-5). The final coded corpus contains 181 records: 159 peer-reviewed conference or journal papers, 9 preprints and 13 standards, specifications, books, technical reports or official guidance documents (p. 5). Each record was coded along eight dimensions (domain, operational task, autonomy role, tool surface, evidence type, evaluation setting, safety control, contribution type), followed by backward and forward snowballing until saturation of the coding scheme (p. 5). Raw hit counts are deliberately not reported because Google Scholar and standards pages lack stable exportable hit sets (p. 5).

Secondary evidence only - this survey executes no empirical comparison of its own and reports no primary MTTD/MTTR reductions. It treats detection and recovery times as the operational objective ('organizations aim to minimise detection and recovery times', SS I, p. 2; improving 'diagnostic and mitigation times' as the measurable goal, SS I.A(d), p. 3) and, most usefully for this review, operationalises them as workflow-level evaluation metrics: Table VI defines MTTD(proxy) as time from incident start to first correct triage signal or first discriminating query, and MTTR(proxy) as time to verified mitigation in sandbox/replay or time to approved plan in a human-gated setting (SS VII.A, Table VI, p. 32). 'Improved MTTR with bounded regressions' is set as the success criterion of the closed-loop self-healing rung (Table III, p. 18), and 'time to mitigate' is listed among the operational outcome observables (SS IV.C, p. 19). Secondary evidence cited from primaries: Xpert's LLM query recommendation reduces time-to-signal in a large-scale incident workflow (SS VI.C(a), p. 27), while ITBench reports current agents succeed on only 13.8% of SRE tasks and 25.2% of CISO tasks across 94 scenarios (SS VII.E, p. 34) - which the survey reads as a warning that demonstrated capability does not yet translate into dependable MTTD/MTTR gains.

Field: General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Agent Systems
Extraction: The survey supplies shared vocabulary and evaluation discipline for the agentic-operations field: the autonomy ladder, assurance contracts, evidence traces, verification wall, budgets and stop rules, positioned explicitly against prior AIOps, LLM4AIOps, network-automation, LLM-agent, RAG and benchmark surveys (SS I.D and Table I, pp. 6-7). It reframes tools as trust boundaries and audit objects rather than mere capability extensions (SS I.D, p. 6; SS II.E(e), pp. 12-13), proposes a five-level evaluation-realism ladder (static QA, tool-use trace replay, sandbox execution, live testbed, canary/rollback-aware evaluation; SS VII.E, pp. 32-34) with a standard report card (Fig. 10, p. 33) and a metrics glossary (Table VI, p. 32), and gives a threat model for agents near control surfaces with a threat-to-control matrix covering prompt injection, RAG poisoning/jamming, telemetry manipulation, excessive agency and exfiltration (Fig. 12, p. 36; Table VII, p. 37). A research agenda recasts open problems as contract-satisfaction questions (Table VIII, p. 42). Multi-agent coordination per se is not the unit of analysis; roles are rungs of a single gated agentic pipeline, with representative systems (DeepLog, Xpert, RCACopilot, RCAgent, TraceRCA, TADBench) mapped onto those rungs (Table IV, p. 30).

Stated method limits: many operational agent systems are deployed inside companies and described only through engineering reports or not at all, and the LLM-agent literature is changing quickly, so the authors separate stable claims from current observations (SS I.C, p. 5); raw search hit counts are not reported (p. 5); the autonomy-raises-failure-severity design rule is qualitative rather than an empirical measurement (SS IV.E, p. 20). The paper is an arXiv preprint, not yet peer-reviewed (p. 1). The open-problems agenda (SS IX, pp. 39-42; Table VIII, p. 42) lists future work: compositional safety across layers and rollout time, benchmark realism and reproducibility for contract-based evaluation, hybrid causal-LLM operations, security and integrity as contract clauses (confused-deputy tool misuse, injection, poisoning), human factors and accountability, minimal interoperable schemas for tool calls/evidence/diffs/approvals/rollback/audit, and continual operation under drift and cost. The conclusion cautions that public benchmarks rarely capture drift, partial observability, stale documentation, tool failure and adversarial inputs, so claims about closed-loop autonomy should remain modest, while read-only support is already valuable (SS X, p. 43).

High-value foundational secondary source for a thesis on an agentic copilot reducing MTTD/MTTR in incident response. It explicitly defines the copilot as the read-only rung of the autonomy ladder, with success criteria of faster evidence location and fewer missed signals under bounded tool budgets (Table III, p. 18; Pattern A, p. 20), and it supplies ready-made, citable operational definitions of MTTD(proxy) and MTTR(proxy) for evaluating such a copilot (Table VI, p. 32), plus the evaluation-realism ladder and report card for designing a defensible measurement protocol (SS VII.E, pp. 32-34; Fig. 10, p. 33). The assurance-contract framing (what the copilot may observe and propose, which gates and audits apply) and the threat model ground the thesis's safety and governance discussion (SS IV.A, pp. 16-17; Table VII, p. 37). Under rule R1 it enters the corpus as a conditional-foundational secondary study: citable for taxonomy, metric definitions, evaluation protocol and safety requirements, but not as primary evidence of MTTD/MTTR effect sizes, since it performs no empirical comparison of its own (SS I.C, pp. 4-5).

High - the most comprehensive secondary source in the corpus mapping Agentic AI onto NetOps/AIOps incident workflows, with an explicit copilot-rung definition and operational MTTD/MTTR proxy metrics directly reusable by the thesis (Table III, p. 18; Table VI, p. 32). Scored as foundational-conditional because it is a preprint survey of 181 records with no primary empirical MTTD/MTTR evidence of its own (p. 1; SS I.C, p. 5).
